- [USER] User inquired about George Washington's ownership of slaves.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] George Washington owned slaves, inheriting his first at the age of 11 and acquiring more throughout his life, totaling over 300 at his death.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Washington began to question the morality of slavery and freed some slaves in his will.
- [USER] User asked why George Washington did not free all of his slaves and who the slaves were that he did not free at his death.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Washington did not free all his slaves because it was common for plantation owners to keep slaves as property and pass them down to heirs.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Washington was concerned about the economic loss from freeing all his slaves, as they were a significant labor source on his estate.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Washington's will freed some slaves and provided for the emancipation of those who served him for at least 30 years or were over the age of 60.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The freed slaves were to be "bound to service" until the age of 26 for males and 24 for females.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Washington left 123 slaves in the custody of his wife, Martha, instructing her to provide for them but not to free them.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] After Washington's death, Martha freed some slaves and kept others as inherited property.
- [USER] User asked when the slaves inherited by Martha were completely freed.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant does not have information on when the slaves inherited by Martha Washington were completely freed.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The legal process for freeing slaves was complex and often required going to court, which could be costly and time-consuming.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Martha Washington passed away in 1802, and many states had laws requiring freed slaves to leave the state within a certain period or risk re-enslavement.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Some slaves inherited by Martha may have been freed gradually or in accordance with her will, but the assistant does not have exact information on this case.
- [USER] User asked if Martha may have intentionally kept some slaves to protect them from re-enslavement.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] It is possible that Martha Washington kept some slaves to protect them from re-enslavement due to laws requiring freed slaves to leave the state.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant noted that owning slaves was common at the time, and it is unclear what Martha's intentions were.
